newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania wants foreign troop deployment speeded up.
newsitem.headline: Albania wants foreign troop deployment speeded up.

text.p: Albania voiced concern on Monday about the slow pace of plans to deploy an Italian-led force in the anarchic state as Rome's government faced political turmoil over sending troops.
"There is a little concern," Foreign Minister Arjan Starova told Reuters. "We'd like a speedy action...we want this force as soon as possible.

"But I have no doubt they will come," Starova said of the planned contingent of up to 6,000 troops. Italy has said the force, approved by the U.N. Security Council on March 28, will start arriving in the week starting April 14.

In Rome, Italy's Communist Refoundation party confirmed that it would break ranks with the centre-left government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi and vote against deployment of the force, codenamed "Alba", the Italian for "sunrise".

Prodi is certain of victory in parliamentary votes on Tuesday and Wednesday because of opposition backing for the force, but it will be the first time that his majority has split on a major policy vote in his 11 months of office.

In the central Albanian village of Levan, about 2,000 people attended a funeral for two sisters who drowned in the Adriatic after a collision between their refugee boat and an Italian corvette on March 28.
Sobbing mourners threw gifts and packages of clothes onto the coffins in the graves as Dituri and Vjollca Kacupi, both in their 30s, were buried. A brother threw in a watch and a ring.
Only four bodies were recovered after the sinking. Tirana says at least 80 people died and 34 survived. Another man who drowned was buried in Fier on Sunday.
Prodi was due to visit rebel-held Vlore -- the southern port from which the refugee boat left and a port the Italian-led force is meant to secure -- in coming days, Starova said.
Prodi agreed to the visit on a tightly-guarded trip to another southern town last week, where he met Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.
Three people were killed at the weekend in gun battles around Vlore, held by rebels after last month's armed uprising, sparked by anger over the collapse of popular savings schemes this year.
Doctors said four Vlore children were injured playing with detonators. They amputated the hand of one of the boys, aged 6.
Starova said states taking part in the force were still debating where each nation would send troops. The forces plan to secure the northern port of Durres, Vlore and Tirana airport for supplies.

"There are certain problems around the deployment of forces," he said, adding: "I think they will find a consensus." Athens is at odds with Rome over which country's troops in the multinational force will be deployed where.
Italy is expected to provide between 2,000 and 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Romania 400 and Spain 300. Austria and Denmark say they are also considering participation.

More than 100 people, mostly pensioners, laid flowers on a monument in Durres on Monday to commemorate the 58th anniversary of the invasion of Albania by Italian troops under fascist leader Benito Mussolini on April 7, 1939.
But for many Albanians, scarred by a Stalinist dictatorship after the war, the anniversary has little significance.

A U.N. relief agency was planning to send a shipment of 340 tonnes of flour to Albania on April 12, the Albanian news agency ATA said. The U.N. estimates that 400,000 of Albania's 3.4 million people may be threatened by food shortages.
Tirana was also searching for toxic chemicals and radioactive materials, some of them used in radar, that it said were stolen from four military arsenals last month.
